question: What is the primary function of the immune system?

options.A: Filtering waste products from the bloodstream
options.B: Defending the body against harmful invaders
options.C: Pumping oxygen-rich blood through blood vessels
options.D: Breaking down food nutrients for energy absorption

explanation: The main job of the immune system is to protect the body from harmful pathogens like bacteria and viruses. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h1)

question: How does the immune system avoid attacking the body's own healthy cells?

options.A: By distinguishing between self and non-self
options.B: By keeping normal cells locked inside deep organs
options.C: By neutralizing all foreign molecules instantly
options.D: By coating healthy cells in thick mucus layers

explanation: You've got this! The immune system is smart—it recognizes the body's own tissues as 'self' and foreign invaders as 'non-self' so it doesn't cause friendly fire. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h1)

question: Which type of immunity are you born with?
explanation: Great job! Innate immunity is your natural, built-in defense system that you are born with. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h2)

question: What is the special superpower of adaptive immunity that innate immunity doesn't have?

options.A: Absence of specialized white blood cells
options.D: Reliance solely on intact skin barriers

explanation: Exactly! Adaptive immunity remembers specific past infections, giving you long-term protection if you meet the same germ again. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h2)

question: Where in the body do T-lymphocytes go to mature?
explanation: Spot on! The thymus gland is the special training school where T-cells go to mature and get ready for action. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h3)

question: What is the main job of secondary lymphoid organs like lymph nodes?

options.A: Regulating the total volume of red blood cells
options.B: Filtering pathogens and housing mature immune cells
options.C: Releasing digestive enzymes into the bloodstream
options.D: Producing brand new stem cells for the blood

explanation: You nailed it! Lymph nodes act like security checkpoints that trap germs from body fluids and launch a coordinated defense. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h3)

question: What do we call any foreign substance that triggers an immune response?
explanation: Well done! Antigens are foreign molecules that wave a red flag and provoke an immune reaction from your body. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h4)

question: Which specific cells are directly responsible for producing antibodies?
explanation: Correct! When B-lymphocytes meet an antigen, they transform into plasma cells, which act as antibody factories. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h4)

question: Which chemical is released during tissue injury to make blood vessels widen?
explanation: That's right! Histamine is released by injured cells to widen blood vessels so white blood cells can rush to the rescue. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h5)

question: Why does an injured or infected area swell up?

options.A: Nerve endings shut down completely to stop pain signals
options.B: Fluid and white blood cells leak into the tissue
options.C: Blood vessels constrict to block all local circulation
options.D: Red blood cells multiply rapidly inside the skin layers

explanation: Spot on! When blood vessels become leaky, fluid and immune cells rush into the tissue, causing that familiar swelling. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h5)

question: What is the main goal of giving a patient a vaccine?

options.A: To replace missing vitamins and minerals in the blood
options.B: To permanently destroy all white blood cells in circulation
options.C: To instantly cure an active chronic bacterial infection
options.D: To stimulate immune memory without causing severe disease

explanation: Exactly! Vaccines safely introduce weak or dead germs so your immune system can build memory without making you sick. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h6)

question: What happens when a vaccinated person later encounters the real pathogen?

options.A: Severe illness develops because memory cells fade away
options.B: The body takes weeks to recognize the foreign invader
options.C: The immune system mistakes it for a harmless body cell
options.D: A fast and strong secondary immune response occurs

explanation: Great work! Because of prior vaccination, your immune system recognizes the germ instantly and fights it off before you get sick. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h6)

question: Which of these conditions is an example of an autoimmune disease?
explanation: You got it! Lupus is an autoimmune disease where the body's immune system gets confused and attacks its own healthy tissues. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h7)

question: How would you describe an immunodeficiency disorder?

options.A: A complete absence of red blood cells in the body
options.B: An overactive immune response directed against food items
options.C: A sudden surge in antibody production during exercise
options.D: An underactive immune system prone to severe infections

explanation: Spot on! Immunodeficiency simply means the immune system is weak and struggles to protect the body from infections. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h7)

question: Which sign of infection might be missing in a patient with a weak immune system?
explanation: Well done! Because their immune system is weak, immunocompromised patients might not mount a strong fever or visible inflammation. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h8)

question: A nurse is caring for a patient with severe neutropenia (low white blood cells). Which food item must be removed from their tray?
explanation: Spot on! Raw, unpeeled fruits can carry harmful bacteria and fungi, which are very dangerous for a patient with low white blood cells. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T14#GNS111_U2_T14_h8)
